newsitem.title: USA: May construction spending drop steepest in three years.
newsitem.headline: May construction spending drop steepest in three years.

text.p: Spending on new construction tumbled at the sharpest rate in more than three years during May, the Commerce Department said on Tuesday, as both government and private-sector projects were scaled back.
The 1.8 percent decline to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $585 billion during May followed a sharply revised 0.3 percent gain in April to $595.7 billion.

Previously, Commerce said that April spending had fallen 1 percent. But the department revised the dollar figures for monthly spending for every month this year, in some cases resulting in substantial changes.
For example, it now says that construction spending was running at a $577.1-billion annual rate in January rather than the $588.9-billion pace it reported a month ago.
During May, spending on both private-sector projects and on public, or government-financed projects, weakened from April.
That was contrary to Wall Street economists' forecasts that May spending would rise 0.5 percent from April.
Public construction spending dropped 5.9 percent in May to $131.3 billion a year -- the steepest decrease since a 6.1 percent plunge in January 1994 -- after a 1.1 percent drop in April.
Spending weakened on highways and streets, water treatment plants and on hospitals and schools during May.
On the private-sector side, construction spending was down 0.5 percent overall to a rate of $453.7 billion in May after a 0.7 percent increase in April.

Spending on new housing projects fell to a rate of $183.3 billion a year from $184.2 billion in April. All the decline was in construction of single-family homes, where spending eased to $159.8 billion in May from $161.6 billion in April.
Exceptionally mild weather earlier in the year may have caused homebuilders to move up the start of some construction projects, possibly borrowing spending from May and later months.
After allowing for inflation, total construction spending was down 2.2 percent in May to a seasonally adjusted $495.9 billion annual rate after being flat in April, the department said.
